title: Beyond Components: Designing Generative UI for MCP Apps — Ruben Casas, Postman

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on MCP apps as a protocol for delivering generative UI, covering tool calling, sandboxing, authentication, and message passing as core protocol features. The content addresses builder-facing tools and protocols (MCP apps, AG UI, JSON Render) applicable across application verticals. The speaker repeatedly emphasizes we are still early and lack imagination for what agent interaction can become. Requires familiarity with React, MCP, and agent orchestration but remains accessible to practitioners. Conference presentation delivered at an AI Engineer channel event. summary: Ruben Casas, staff engineer at Postman, examines the gap between rapidly improving model capabilities for UI generation and the still-static UI paradigms used by most agents. He traces a trajectory from November 2022, when developers copy-pasted code from ChatGPT ("poor man's bit coding"), through a late-2025 inflection point driven by models like GPT 5.2 and Opus 4.5 that produce high-fidelity, thoughtful UI code. When he prompted such a model to rewrite his blog, it added a search box with blur animation and accessibility features without being asked—convincing him the model writes better frontend code than he does. He frames the current moment using Andrej Karpathy's analogy: we have a new computer where interaction feels like talking to a terminal; the GUI has not yet been invented. Two open questions emerge: where the UI runs (chat embedded everywhere vs. a single super app via MCP apps) and what the model generates. He maps three levels of UI generation. Static UI passes props to predefined React components—examples include the AG UI protocol and Goose Auto Visualizer. Declarative UI has the LLM generate JSON, YAML, or Python descriptors that a rendering engine maps to existing components—examples include Vercel's JSON Render and Netflix's server-driven personalization. He argues declarative UI is the best balance today, offering flexibility, design-system consistency, predictability, speed, and token efficiency. Fully generative UI skips components: the model writes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on demand. His Postman weather-agent experiment does this in a single tool call, producing imaginative UI with no prebuilt components. The catch is trust: LLM-generated code needs containment and sandboxing. He identifies MCP apps—with authentication, tool calling, message passing, and a double-iframe sandbox—as the ideal delivery mechanism, noting Anthropic chose MCP apps for its own first-party visualizer. He closes with the TV/radio analogy: early TV shows were radio shows with cameras, and we similarly lack imagination for what agent interaction can become. He extends this into a forward-looking vision: the future beyond components is collaborative and personalized, exemplified by the Excalidraw MCP app, which creates a shared canvas where humans and agents interact directly—users can ask the agent to change things while also clicking and modifying the UI themselves. He emphasizes we are still early, do not have the answers, but can shape the future of this new computer.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Models like GPT 5.2 and Opus 4.5 reached an inflection point in late 2025 for high-fidelity UI generation, sometimes producing thoughtful, accessible code unprompted.
Three levels of UI generation exist: static (props to predefined components), declarative (JSON/YAML descriptors mapped to components), and fully generative (model writes HTML/CSS/JS on demand).
Declarative UI is the best balance today—flexible, consistent with design systems, predictable, fast, and token-efficient.
Fully generative UI requires sandboxing and containment because LLM-generated code cannot be blindly trusted.
MCP apps—with authentication, tool calling, message passing, and double-iframe sandboxing—are the ideal delivery mechanism for generative UI.
Anthropic strategically chose MCP apps for its own first-party visualizer, validating the protocol beyond third-party use.
The TV/radio analogy: first TV shows were radio shows with cameras—we lack imagination for what the new medium of agent interaction can become.
The future beyond components is collaborative and personalized human-agent interaction, exemplified by the Excalidraw MCP app's shared canvas where users and agents modify UI together.
We are still early and do not have the answers, but can shape the future of this new computer.

sections.title: Introduction: The evolution from 'poor man's bit coding' to high-fidelity UI generation
sections.summary: Casas traces the journey from copy-pasting ChatGPT code blocks in November 2022 to a late-2025 inflection point with GPT 5.2 and Opus 4.5. He describes prompting a model to rewrite his blog; it unpromptedly created a search box with blur animation and accessibility, convincing him models now write better frontend code than he does.

sections.title: Why are we still stuck with static UI?
sections.summary: Casas asks why, if models are so capable at writing UI code, most agent UIs remain static. He questions the absence of the 'Jarvis moment' with floating UI windows and introduces himself as a staff engineer at Postman working on generative UI and MCP apps.

sections.title: The new computer: Searching for the interface of the future
sections.summary: Using Andrej Karpathy's analogy, Casas frames current AI interaction as talking to a terminal before the GUI was invented. He questions whether chat is the final interface, noting SaaS companies are putting chat everywhere but that chat is not the final UI.

sections.title: The role of MCP apps and 'Super Apps'
sections.summary: Casas presents the super-app concept via MCP apps, where one app like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini renders third-party UI. He distinguishes two separate questions: where the UI runs (chat everywhere vs. super app) versus what the model generates.

sections.title: Three levels of UI generation: Static, Declarative, and Generative
sections.summary: Casas introduces the three-level spectrum: mostly static, declarative, and generative UI, which structures the rest of the talk.

sections.title: Understanding Static UI components (e.g., AG UI, Goose)
sections.summary: Static UI has the agent act as orchestrator, passing props and data to predefined developer-built components that the client renders. Examples include the AG UI protocol SDK (registering client tools mapped to React components) and Goose Auto Visualizer (matching arbitrary data to predefined components).

sections.title: The benefits of Declarative UI (e.g., JSON/YAML renderers)
sections.summary: Declarative UI has the LLM generate JSON, YAML, or Python descriptors that a rendering engine maps to existing static components. Examples include Vercel's JSON Render and Netflix's server-driven personalization. Casas argues this is the best balance today—flexible, consistent with design systems, predictable, fast, and token-efficient.

sections.title: Moving to the next level: Generative UI components
sections.summary: Fully generative UI has the model write HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on demand at runtime. Casas demonstrates a Postman weather agent that calls a weather API, creates a joke, and generates all HTML/CSS/JS in one tool call, producing imaginative UI with no prebuilt components.

sections.title: The challenge of trust: The need for sandboxing and containment
sections.summary: Casas identifies the core problem: if we don't trust third-party code, we shouldn't trust LLM-generated code either. Fully generative UI needs a distribution model with boundaries, containment, and sandboxing.

sections.title: Why MCP apps are the ideal delivery mechanism for Generative UI
sections.summary: MCP apps provide authentication, tool calling, message passing, and sandboxing via double iframe by default. Casas notes Anthropic chose MCP apps for its own first-party visualizer rather than building a custom mechanism, validating the protocol for both first-party and third-party generative UI.

sections.title: The 'TV/Radio' analogy: Imagining the future of agent interaction
sections.summary: Casas compares the current era to early television: the first TV shows were radio shows with cameras because nobody could yet imagine what else to do with the new medium. He argues we are still in the radio era with this new technology and cannot yet imagine what amazing things we will do with the new computer.

sections.title: Beyond components: Towards true human-agent collaboration
sections.summary: Casas speculates that the future will move beyond components toward human-agent collaboration. He highlights the Excalidraw MCP app, which creates a shared canvas where a human and an agent can collaborate—users can ask the agent to change things while also clicking and modifying the UI directly. He envisions generative UI becoming super personalized and collaborative rather than just an orchestrator and delivery mechanism for visualizations.

sections.title: Conclusion: Shaping the future of user interfaces
sections.summary: Casas acknowledges we are still early and do not have the answer to what the future of user interfaces will be. He encourages the audience that we can shape that future and create this new computer, then closes with thanks and an invitation for questions.
